quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on finding the face, the warp direction and the steps of taking a sample apart.

questions.q: Which side of a fabric is usually the face?
options: The side with more loose fibre
Always the side with the weft floats
The side with more lustre and a clearer, better-defined weave
questions.explain: The face normally has more lustre and a sharper weave; finishes and prints are on the face, and warp-faced weaves show their warp floats there.

questions.q: A sample has a selvedge. Which way does the warp run?
options: At right angles to the selvedge
It cannot be told from a selvedge
questions.explain: The selvedge is formed by the weft turning round the outer warp ends, so the warp runs along it.

questions.q: Why do warp yarns usually feel harsher and stiffer than weft yarns?
options: Warp yarns are sized before weaving
questions.explain: Size is applied to the warp to withstand weaving, so warp threads feel stiffer and are harder to unravel; weft is unsized and softer.

questions.q: In a dense fabric the set of threads with more crimp is usually the warp.
questions.explain: The lecture gives this as a guide for dense fabrics, with the caution that in weft-faced cloths it can be the reverse.

questions.q: One set of yarns in a sample is two-fold and the other single. Which is almost always the warp?
questions.explain: Folded yarns are stronger and are put in the warp, which takes the strain of weaving.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a sign of the warp direction?
options: Stripes, cords and the prominent twill line usually run warp-way
Picks per inch are normally higher than ends per inch
Weft yarns are finer and stronger
questions.explain: Design features run warp-way and the sett is normally higher in the warp; weft is usually coarser, softer and unsized.

questions.q: What does 'sett' refer to in fabric analysis?
options: The number of threads per inch or cm in each direction
questions.explain: Sett is the thread density, ends and picks per inch (or cm); the lecture notes it is normally higher in the warp.

questions.q: The lecture says ends and picks should be counted once, at the centre of the sample.
questions.explain: They should be counted in several places and averaged, because sett varies across a piece.

questions.q: What is the purpose of noting each end's interlacing on point paper until the pattern repeats?
options: To find the weave repeat so the cloth can be reproduced
questions.explain: Recording the interlacing until it repeats reveals the weave, from which the draft, peg plan and denting follow.

questions.q: Which four items does the lecture say must be recorded so the fabric can be reproduced?
options: Weave, draft, peg plan and denting
Loom speed, efficiency, healds and reed
questions.explain: The lecture's final step is to record the weave, draft, peg plan and denting; counts and crimp are measured earlier but these four define the construction.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The crimp formula, the count-from-weight idea and the relationships used when a sample is analysed.

questions.q: Which expression gives crimp as a fraction, following the lecture?
questions.explain: Crimp = straightened length ÷ cloth length − 1, equivalent to (straightened − cloth) ÷ cloth. Reversing the ratio gives a negative number.

questions.q: A thread is pulled from the sample and straightened. If the straightened length rises while the cloth length stays the same, the crimp…
questions.explain: More extra length in the thread means more waviness, so crimp rises.

questions.q: Which quantity is found by weighing a measured length of unravelled threads?
questions.explain: Count relates weight to length, so a known length of threads weighed gives the count; crimp and sett are found by other steps.

questions.q: For a direct count system such as tex, a heavier weight for the same length means a coarser yarn.
questions.explain: Tex is grams per 1,000 m, so more weight per length means a higher tex and a coarser yarn; in an indirect system such as Ne the number would fall.

questions.q: Why does the lecture say to confirm the counts with the fabric weight formula from Lecture 2?
options: The formula is needed to find the selvedge
The counts, setts and crimps together must reproduce the measured fabric weight; a mismatch shows an error
The weight formula gives the face side
questions.explain: Fabric weight is built from sett, count and crimp, so the calculated weight checks all the measurements at once.

questions.q: The crimp of the warp threads is 8 %. How much warp yarn length is needed per metre of cloth?
questions.explain: Length of yarn = cloth length × (1 + crimp) = 1 × 1.08 = 1.08 m. Subtracting instead of adding is the common error.

questions.q: If the weft of a sample has far more crimp than the warp, the lecture says the fabric must be faulty.
questions.explain: The lecture notes that in weft-faced cloths the crimp rule can be reversed; it is a guide, not a certainty.

questions.q: When the sett is higher in one direction than the other, which direction is normally the warp?
options: The direction with the higher sett
The direction with the lower sett
The direction with the coarser yarn
It cannot be inferred from sett
questions.explain: The lecture gives a higher sett as a normal property of the warp direction.

questions.q: Ends per cm are measured as 24. What is this in ends per inch, to the nearest whole number?
questions.explain: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, so 24 × 2.54 = 61 ends per inch. Dividing gives 9.4, a reversed conversion.

questions.q: In which order does the lecture place these analysis steps?
options: Find counts, record the construction, count threads, unravel
Measure crimp, count threads, record, unravel
Record the construction first, then everything else
Count threads, unravel and plot the weave, measure crimp, find counts, record the construction
questions.explain: The lecture's list runs: count ends and picks, unravel and note the interlacing, measure crimp, weigh for counts and confirm with the weight formula, then record weave, draft, peg plan and denting.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Averaging thread counts, working out crimp and yarn counts from measurements, and checking fabric weight.

questions.q: Ends per inch are counted in four places as 62, 60, 64 and 62. What is the average ends per inch?
A warp thread 10.0 cm long in the cloth straightens to 10.9 cm. What is its crimp, as a percentage?
A weft thread measured over 20 cm of cloth straightens to 21.2 cm. What is the crimp percentage?
Fifty unravelled and straightened ends, each 25 cm long, together weigh 0.25 g. What is the yarn count in tex? (tex = grams per 1,000 m)
Forty picks, each 30 cm long when straightened, weigh 0.36 g. What is their count in tex?
A yarn is 20 tex. What is its English cotton count Ne, given Ne = 590.5 ÷ tex? Give one decimal.
A fabric has 2,400 ends per metre of width, warp crimp 8 % and warp yarn of 20 tex. What is the warp weight in grams per square metre? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: Warp length per m² = 2,400 × 1.08 = 2,592 m; at 20 g per 1,000 m this weighs 2,592 × 20 ÷ 1,000 = 51.8 g.

questions.q: The same fabric has 2,000 picks per metre of length, weft crimp 6 % and weft of 30 tex. What is the weft weight in grams per square metre? Give one decimal.
A sample is counted as 60 ends per inch in one direction and 48 threads per inch in the other, with no selvedge. Which direction is most probably the warp?
options: The direction with the softer yarn
questions.explain: Sett is normally higher in the warp, so the 60 per inch direction is the likely warp; softer yarn points to weft.

questions.q: An end unravelled from the sample passes over 3 picks and under 1 pick, repeatedly. What weave is this?
questions.explain: Over 3 and under 1 is written 3/1: a warp-faced twill. Reading it as 1/3 reverses face and back.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Sampling-room scenarios: a buyer's swatch arrives and the mill must identify and reproduce it.

questions.q: A swatch arrives cut without a selvedge. Which clue would you test first to find the warp?
options: Feel for the sized, harsher set of threads and check for a two-fold yarn
Measure the width of the swatch
questions.explain: Without a selvedge, size and feel, folded yarns, design direction and crimp are the lecture's clues; weight and width say nothing about direction.

questions.q: A printed sample shows a sharp print on one side and a faint ghost on the other. Which is the face?
options: The side with the sharp print
The side with the faint ghost
The side with the weft floats
questions.explain: Printed or finished fabrics show the finish on the face; the ghost is strike-through on the back.

questions.q: A drill sample shows long warp floats on one side. Which side is the face and what does this suggest about the weave?
options: That side is the face; it is a warp-faced twill
That side is the back; it is a weft-faced sateen
That side is the face; it is plain weave
questions.explain: Warp-faced weaves such as drills and satins show their warp floats on the face.

questions.q: Thread counts taken across a swatch give 58, 66 and 60 ends per inch. What should the analyst do?
options: Take the highest as the specification
Report the lowest to be safe
Average them and, if the spread is large, count more places
questions.explain: The lecture says to count in several places and average; a wide spread calls for more readings, not for picking one.

questions.q: A buyer's sample must be reproduced exactly. After finding the weave, counts and setts, what else must go on the specification sheet?
questions.explain: The lecture ends with recording weave, draft, peg plan and denting so the fabric can be woven again.

questions.q: If the thread counted as weft is clearly the stronger, finer and more uniform yarn, that is a reason to re-check the warp direction.
questions.explain: Warp yarns are generally finer, stronger and more uniform; finding these qualities in the supposed weft suggests the directions were confused.

questions.q: After weighing unravelled threads, the analyst calculates a fabric weight 15 % lower than the swatch actually weighs. What is the sensible conclusion?
options: Increase the crimp figure until it matches
Re-check the counts, setts and crimp, since the weight formula should agree with the sample
questions.explain: The weight formula is a check on all the measurements; a 15 % gap means one of them is in error and should be re-measured, not fudged.

questions.q: Why should a sample be unravelled from both directions rather than just one?
options: Because only picks can be counted
To record the interlacing of ends over picks and confirm the repeat in both directions
questions.explain: Unravelling a few picks and ends lets the analyst see each end's path over the picks and confirm the repeat.

questions.q: A sample whose two sets of threads have identical count, twist and crimp cannot have its warp direction identified at all.
questions.explain: Other clues remain: the direction of stripes, cords or the twill line, the sett, and any selvedge; the lecture gives several independent tests.

questions.q: A cord fabric has pronounced ridges running in one direction. What does this tell you?
options: The sample is a double cloth
The ridges usually run warp-way, so that is the warp direction
questions.explain: The lecture lists stripes, cords and the twill line as normally running warp-way.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that combine the clues and calculations of fabric analysis, including the usual slips.

questions.q: A sample measures 5 cm in the warp direction. The warp threads unravelled from it straighten to 5.6 cm. What is the warp crimp percentage?
A weft yarn of 30 tex has 6 % crimp. How many metres of weft yarn are needed for 1 m² of a cloth with 2,000 picks per metre?
questions.explain: Each pick across a 1 m width takes 1.06 m of yarn; 2,000 picks × 1.06 = 2,120 m.

questions.q: A student computes crimp as cloth length ÷ straightened length − 1 and gets −8 %. What is the correct crimp?
questions.explain: The ratio was inverted. If cloth ÷ straightened = 0.92, then straightened ÷ cloth = 1 ÷ 0.92 = 1.087, so crimp is 8.7 %, not simply 8 %.

questions.q: Thirty straightened ends of 40 cm each weigh 0.24 g. What is the yarn count in tex?
A sample is a dense warp rib with the weft lying almost straight and the warp heavily crimped. Which statement is correct?
options: The crimp clue fails here, since warp ribs put crimp in the weft
A warp rib has no crimp in either direction
The weft must be the two-fold yarn
The crimp clue points to the warp correctly here, since the warp has more crimp
questions.explain: A warp rib puts almost all the crimp in the warp, so the heavily crimped set is indeed the warp; the lecture's caution applies to weft-faced cloths, where the weft may crimp more.

questions.q: A fabric is analysed as 2,400 ends per metre at 20 tex with 8 % crimp, and 2,000 picks per metre at 30 tex with 6 % crimp. What is its total weight in grams per square metre? Give one decimal.
The same fabric's swatch actually weighs 118 g/m². What does the comparison with the calculated 115.4 g/m² suggest?
options: The sample must be a double cloth
The measurements are consistent within about 2 %, allowing for size and finish on the yarn
The warp count must be wrong by half
questions.explain: A 2 % gap is within normal error and the extra weight of size or finish; a large gap would call for re-measurement.

questions.q: Because the warp is sized, it is the weft that is easier to unravel from a grey sample.
questions.explain: Size stiffens the warp and makes it harder to pull out; the softer unsized weft comes away more easily.

questions.q: A sample with a 2/2 twill has its twill line running from bottom-left to top-right on the face. A student records the weave while looking at the back. What error results?
options: The number of healds is doubled
The sett is counted in cm
The twill direction is recorded reversed
questions.explain: Viewed from the back a twill line slopes the other way, so the recorded direction would be wrong; the weave should be plotted from the face.

questions.q: Which single clue would most reliably settle the warp direction in an unsized, finished, balanced plain cloth?
options: A selvedge, if any part of one is present
questions.explain: Size, crimp, sett and feel may be similar in a balanced finished cloth; a selvedge is definitive because the warp always runs parallel to it.
